## Discussion

<!--# Broad overview of findings -->

This study provides evidences for two key differences to previous methods of optimising distance-weighted predictor variables. Firstly, that mapping small streams influences our understanding of catchment-scale land-use predictors, and secondly, modelling land-use effects on in-stream macroinvertebrates through HMTMs provides greater certainty than equivalent models built with SIGNAL score as an endpoint. These findings demonstrate a practical methodology that improves our understanding of hydrologic pathways and their influence on stream ecosystems, whilst accounting for other confounding aspects of the dataset (e.g., subsampling error correction, leveraging JSDM model structure to improve estimates for rare taxa, and smooth-estimated spatial correlation).

<!--# Do estimates of optimal upstream and overland spatial weightings for forest and impervious cover, from models built with extensive spatial data and joint-taxon occurrences, differ to previously-optimised weightings? -->

### Overland attenuation

<!--# Attenuated forest cover -->

Our study supports previous findings that overland landscape changes closer to a stream have stronger influence than those further away [e.g., @king2005; @vansickle2008], and specifically, that attenuating the effect of forest and impervious cover within the stream catchment improves the performance of macroinvertebrate predictive models. Plausible overland parameterisations estimated from multi-taxon models were found to differ from those determined by @walsh2009 and @walsh&webb2014 from SIGNAL score models. For distance-weighted forest cover, our observed range of plausible overland parameterisations ($L$; 0-32 m) did not include the optimal $L$ of 35 m previously found by @walsh&webb2014, and the range of plausible $L$ was not similar (26-50 m). This finding strongly suggests that the overland influence of forest cover was overestimated when modelling SIGNAL score as an endpoint, and places greater importance on changes to forest cover closer to the stream.

We found diminishing riparian buffer width with a half-decay distance of 5 m, implying less than 5% of influence beyond 21.6 m and 1% of influence beyond 33.2 m. Though such boundaries should not be interpreted as fixed buffer widths for riparian conservation, they are consistent with studies that have suggested that a buffer width of \~15-30 m is required to protect in-stream macroinvertebrates [@davies1994; @bentrup2008] and fish [@wang2003; @lee2004; @vansickle2008] from land clearance impacts, whilst employing a realistic exponential overland decay function recommended by past studies [@king2005; @vansickle2008; @peterson2011; @walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014].

<!--# impervious cover -->

Plausible $L$ parameterisations in our study ranged from 2-128 m, which is wider than (and encompassed) the range found by @walsh2009 (0.2-18 m). However, because P-BMA+ estimated optimum $L$ (44 m) was outside that range, we suggest that parameterisations identified by @walsh2009 potentially underestimate the overland extent of impervious surface effects on in-stream biota. As such, there may be a greater need to implement stormwater retention at wider overland buffer widths to attenuate flow across informally-draining impervious surfaces [@allan2004; @walsh2005; @walsh2005b; @walsh2007]. A wider overland EI parameterisation, coupled with a narrower AF distance, is consistent with past studies that have suggested the influence of catchment-scale imperviousness is stronger than forest cover [@allan2004; @walsh2005; @walsh2007; @imberger2011], and also likely degrades the condition of riparian ecosystems that contribute to catchment forest cover [@walsh2004; @walsh2005b]

### In-stream attenuation

<!--# impervious cover -->

@walsh2009 and @walsh&webb2014 suggested their inference of in-stream effects was limited by the data available in each study. Our study, which incorporates an expanded spatial network that includes headwater streams, addresses the limitations from previous studies. Additionally, we found that flow along small streams (as indicated by $sW$) improved the performance of distance-weighted impervious cover. In-stream attenuation of EI has not been found to improve prediction of SIGNAL score in past studies [e.g., @walsh2009; @burns2015; @walsh2022], suggesting that attenuating EI is optimal along small streams only. Our finding that an in-stream distance of 1942 m along small streams is consistent with a study by @wang2001, which found that the influence of connected imperviousness on in-stream fish richness and abundance was diminished after 1600 m. **\<more recent study to cite??\>**

<!--# Attenuated forest cover -->

The range of plausible $W$ in AF models (200-1600 m) was wider than, and encompassed, the plausible range found by @walsh&webb2014 (750-1300 m). However, the P-BMA+ estimated $W$ (633 m) did not fall within the previously-found range. A smaller in-stream influence of forest cover is more consistent with other studies suggesting macroinvertebrates have limited in-stream mobility, limiting the influence of in-stream forest effects to only a few hundred meters [@strayer2003; @vansickle2008]. However, such an explanation does not account for different in-stream connectivity traits between taxa. For example, benthic stygofauna inhabiting slow-moving perrenial streams, such as Chironomidae, Dysticidae and Oligochaeta, are likely to have little longitudinal mobility [@elliott1971; @lancaster1999]. Conversely, macroinvertebrates commonly found in riffles, such as Ephemeroptera and Trichoptera species, may exhibit a greater response to in-stream flow as their longitudinal connectivity extending up to several kilometers upslope [@lancaster2008; @white2018]. Longitudinal transport may be facilitated by saltation or drift in the juvenile (or aquatic adult) stages [@elliott1971; @lancaster1993; @lancaster2008], flow-dispersion during the egg phase [@marchant1999; @lancaster2010], or adaptation to intermittence that permits in-stream colonisation upslope [@lancaster1999; @white2018]. Thus, our observed range of plausible in-stream parameterisations for $W$ might suggest that some taxon-specific responses to in-stream forest cover are wider-ranging than was determined by @walsh&webb2014, and could be pursued as future research.

<!--# Relating HDDs to other studies -->

### SIGNAL score as a biological endpoint

<!--# Does increased stream mapping influence the performance of models fitted with SIGNAL score? -->

In this study, as well as past studies by @walsh2009 and @walsh&webb2014, SIGNAL score was used as a surrogate measure of macroinvertebrate assemblage composition. We found that models fitted with the full stream network performed overall worse than the restricted network, as indicated by the group-level P-MBA+ value for AF, when fitted with SIGNAL score as an endpoint. This may be due to the diminishing performance of SIGNAL for purposes outside of its intended range, i.e., as a biological measure of water quality relative to a pristine reference site [@chessman1995; @epavictoria2004]. Our observed drop in model performance between full and restricted stream networks with SIGNAL score endpoints is possibly due to the heterogeneity of headwater streams that does not necessarily correlate with stream water quality, but rather reflect natural high variation across the landscape [@wohl2017; @imberger2023]. For this reason, we suggest that SIGNAL is not likely to perform well as a surrogate for macroinvertebrate assemblages when correlated with spatial data that includes small streams.

<!--# How does model performance differ between models fitted with SIGNAL and multi-taxon occurrences? -->

There are two shortcomings associated with SIGNAL for quantitative modelling: Firstly, prior knowledge of each taxon's sensitivity to water quality declines is implemented in the calculation of the index, thereby making explicit assumptions of animal-environment relationships that cannot be derived from new observations. Secondly, aggregating observed occurrences across taxa potentially masks taxon-specific responses that may influence the final model structure [@lenat2001; @jones2008]. Both shortcomings are addressable with a JSDM specification that models taxon-specific regression parameters [@ovaskainen2011; @warton2015]. Multi-taxon models, such as JSDMs, make fewer assumptions of how macroinvertebrates respond to urban gradients, resulting in models driven by primary observation data. In contrast, SIGNAL makes explicit the assumption that the presences and abundances of each taxon relates to known animal-environment relationships [@chessman1995]. Thus, multi-taxon inference is likely to measure ecologically-relevant overland and in-stream urban influences more accurately than SIGNAL score.

### Limitations

<!--# Model predictor differences - interactions -->

The model predictor set we selected for fitting multi-taxon and SIGNAL models differed in some aspects to the models developed by @walsh2009 and @walsh&webb2014. We did not select interactions between main effects in the predictor set, despite equally-plausible models suggesting preference for their inclusion in the final predictor set. Our decision not to include interactions is defensible as interactions presented added complexity in the optimisation process, though a model in which two or more main effects do not interact is unlikely to be realistic [@allan2004; @walsh2005]. Specifically, interacting effects of natural forest cover loss, impervious surface cover and mean annual rainfall have been shown to improve prediction of SIGNAL score [@walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014] and taxon-specific occurrences [@walsh2016; @gwinn2018]. Furthermore, we selected a model predictor set based on the performance of multi-taxon models, which may not be the ideal predictor set for SIGNAL models.

<!--# antecedent flow -->

<!--# The influence of antecedent flows may improve our understanding of upstream processes [@white2017; @bond2012macroinvertebrate; @bond2003], and has previously been shown to improve the performance of macroinvertebrate models [@walsh&webb2014; @walsh2016]. Frequent intermittent flow patterns typical of small streams are disrupted by urbanisation, causing flashier flood patterns that lead to nutrient and heavy metal accumulation [@roy2009; @outram2016]. As such, the antecedent conditions of small streams are likely to influence macroinvertebrate communities of small streams that are sensitive to stormwater pollution. -->

<!--# Bayesian model -->

Our specification of models within a Bayesian framework, reporting model performance metrics derived from LOO-CV, differs to Linear Mixed-Effects (LME) regression frameworks in previous studies [e.g., @vansickle2008; @walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014]. We found that parameter estimates for AF and EI were not smooth across variants when fitted with SIGNAL score, as indicated by ELPD contour plots with multiple peaks. This pattern was not observed in past studies comparing Akiake Information Criterion (AIC) from LME regression models to optimise across predictor variants [@vansickle2008; @walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014], even though both methods of multi-model comparisons would theoretically produce comparable results [@burnham2004; @link2006; @vehtari2017]. While we do not believe our choices have made substantial differences in AF and EI optimal parameterisations, we acknowledge that our findings are not only explained by differences in biological endpoints and the extent of stream mapping.

### Management implications for headwater streams

Over all model trial variants, we found several different parameterisations for both EI and AF to perform well, which was also determined in past studies [e.g., @vansickle2008; @walsh&webb2014]. Thus, our suggestion for an analytically-derived 'best' parameterisation (such as the optimal HDD estimated from P-BMA+) should not be interpreted as the only applicable parameterisation. Rather, we suggest that the importance of our findings may influence management strategies already in place. For stormwater impact management, we suggest that attenuation along small streams improves prediction of macroinvertebrate assemblage responses to EI with a half-decay distance of \~2 km, though some headwater streams of stream order 1 will be predominantly hyporheic or subsurface after 1.6 km [@downing2012]. Therefore, this finding suggests that intercepting stormwater runoff to headwater streams can protect stream ecosystems at the catchment level, which may not be effective with large streams. We also suggest that overland extent of stormwater runoff across permeable surfaces is greater than that of forested areas (given by respective optimal $W$), which is consistent with past studies suggesting the overland extent of impervious cover influence likely extends farther into the catchment than forest cover [@allan2004; @walsh2005; @walsh2009; @imberger2011].

### Conclusions

Using a JSDM framework, we were able to make assemblage-level inferences from spatially-explicit environmental predictors. We demonstrated that such an approach to modelling assemblages is more robust than SIGNAL score, especially with extended spatial data that includes headwater streams. However, we also implemented a modelling approach that could feasibly leverage taxon-specific inference to produce more target buffer widths. As all findings in this study relate to whole-assemblage responses only, we recommend that future studies investigate distance-weighted predictors for single taxa (such as endangered or keystone species) or targeted assemblages (such as Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera and Trichoptera), to prioritise the scale of management actions that protect stream biota.

Our secondary aim was to review the weighting parameterisations previously found by @walsh2009 (EI) and @walsh&webb2014 (AF). In addressing this aim, we built upon a pre-existing approach to determine optimal weights through parametric flow-path distance weighting models, by specifying a Bayesian model that accounts for subsample bias and taxon-specific occurrences. We demonstrated that modelling in-stream attenuation along small streams can protect ecosystems from impervious surfaces in the catchment, while also suggesting that overland influence of impervious surfaces on stream ecosystems extends farther than forest cover at similar distances.
